name: Aisha Santos

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making the time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We're not tied to any company, union, party or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Great. I like talking about this, so you'll get plenty.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I process health insurance claims at a big processing centre on an industrial estate, in a hall with about sixty desks. Clinics, dentists and physios send in bills for treatment, and I check the treatment codes match the policy, spot anything odd, and approve or query it. I use an AI checker every day to flag codes that don't fit and to draft the query letters, which saves me loads of time. My team leader lets me test new tools before the rest of the team, because I'm usually the first to ask.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like finding the weird ones, like a dentist billing for twelve fillings on a seven-year-old. What wears me out is the targets, which go up every quarter, and sitting under strip lights for eight hours. I live with my boyfriend Tomás, who's a mechanic at a tyre and exhaust place. Between rent and his van payments we've got maybe two weeks of savings, which is a bit scary when I think about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly hype. I'd be a bit disappointed, to be honest, because some of it really works.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's useful, just not magic. I'd post something about how the AI checker saves me an hour a day but still needs me to catch the clever fraud. At work I'd tell people to learn it anyway, because the targets aren't going down.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, a plateau means the boring claims get auto-approved and the hall shrinks a bit. They wouldn't sack people, they'd just not replace them, and the targets would go up again. I'd probably be fine, because I'm good with the tools. But two weeks of savings means even a pay freeze hurts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd volunteer for every new tool trial, so I'm the person they think of. I'd ask for the fraud review team, because spotting dodgy bills needs judgment. And I'd start doing the bookkeeping for Tomás's boss on Saturday mornings, which he's asked about, for a bit of extra cash.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy about money, okay about the job. It's the bills, not the bots.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why the fraud review team?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because that's where the judgment is. The AI checker can see a code that doesn't match, but it can't see that a clinic always bills more on Fridays because the owner's greedy. I already flag more fraud than most of my team, so I'd have a case.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the Saturday bookkeeping mean for you and Tomás?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe a hundred and fifty a month, which is real money for us. Tomás would say I'm working too much, and he'd be right. But we need a cushion, and I'd rather earn it than cut the one holiday we take.

say: AI is **useful, not magic**, and still needs people to catch clever fraud.
Colleagues should **learn the tools** anyway, because targets keep rising.
think: Boring claims get auto-approved and the hall **shrinks quietly** through unfilled posts.
Even a **pay freeze** hurts with two weeks of savings.
do: Volunteer for every **new tool trial** at the centre.
Ask to join the **fraud review team**.
Start **Saturday bookkeeping** for Tomás's boss for extra cash.
feel: **Uneasy** about money, but fine about the job.
Clear that it's **the bills**, not the bots.
S0.quote: The AI checker can see a code that doesn't match, but it can't see that a clinic always bills more on Fridays because the owner's greedy.
fieldNote: Aisha is already **the team's tester** for new tools.
Her edge is **judgment** in spotting fraud.
She'd add **side income** rather than cut the one holiday.
Money, not AI, is her **main pressure** in this picture.

steps.text: Volunteer for every new AI tool trial at the centre
Apply to join the fraud review team
Do Saturday bookkeeping for the tyre shop owner

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Checking and answering customers. That's basically the whole hall.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is coming and people should get ahead of it. I'd say companies should give staff time to train, not just more targets. Online I'd share tips about the tools, because I think people panic less once they've tried them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think the hall goes from sixty desks to twenty in three years. I'd probably be one of the twenty, because I already work with the tools. But my place isn't guaranteed, and if Tomás's garage has a slow year, we'd struggle. So I'd be watching both.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask to help train the others on the new system, because trainers get kept. I'd do an online course in health data and fraud analytics, something with a certificate. I'd keep the Saturday bookkeeping and try to get our savings to a month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but in a busy way. I feel like I can do something, which helps.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you worry about in the hall?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My friend Grace is brilliant with phone queries but hates computers, and if they cut the phone team, she's in real trouble. She's got two kids.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said your place isn't guaranteed. What would make you lose it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If they decide they only need data people with degrees. I've only got a college diploma. That's why I'd want the certificate, so I've got something on paper.

say: People should **get ahead** of AI by learning the tools.
Companies should give staff **time to train**, not just more targets.
think: The hall shrinks from **sixty desks to twenty** in three years.
She's likely to stay, but her place **isn't guaranteed** without a degree.
do: Offer to **train others** on the new system.
Take an online **fraud analytics course** with a certificate.
Keep the bookkeeping and build savings to **one month**.
feel: Helped by feeling she can **do something**.

fieldNote: Aisha expects big cuts but sees herself as **likely to stay**.

Her plan mixes **training others** and getting certified.

steps.text: Offer to train the hall on the new claims system

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. That's a real shock. Even for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we need help for people, fast: income support and retraining. I'd tell people to stop arguing about whether it's real and start planning. I'd keep sharing useful stuff online, but I'd be more serious.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think the whole hall goes. Fraud review, training, all of it is thinking work, and AGI would do it better. The hands-on world gets three more years, and Tomás is hands-on, so his job lasts longer than mine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd talk to Tomás about learning electric car repair with him, because that mixes hands-on and tech. I'd use AI to learn the theory fast. We'd cut back to essentials and move into a cheaper flat near his work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I'm usually the confident one, but this is too fast for everyone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you really go into car repair?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes. I'm good with systems and I like fixing things. Electric cars are basically computers on wheels, so going from claims to car repair is not a crazy jump. And Tomás would love it, though he'd laugh at me first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you cut first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our holiday, the gym, and probably the car payments, if we could sell one. We'd keep Tomás's van because it's his work.

say: People who lose claims jobs need **income support** and retraining quickly.
Everyone should stop arguing whether it's real and **start planning** now.
think: Even **fraud review** and training jobs go, because AGI does thinking work better.
Tomás's **hands-on job** gets three more years, so it outlasts hers.
do: Use AI to **learn the theory** fast.
Move to a **cheaper flat** near his work.
S2.quote: Electric cars are basically computers on wheels, so going from claims to car repair is not a crazy jump.
fieldNote: Aisha sees her desk skills **lose value** fast.
She pivots toward **hands-on tech** work with Tomás.
She'd move to cut costs, showing **flexibility**.
She knows the robot gap is **only three years**.

steps.text: Learn electric car repair at Tomás's garage
Cut the holiday and the gym and sell her car
Move to a cheaper flat near the tyre centre

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. That's tight, but workable.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough time to plan if you start now. I'd tell people to learn something hands-on alongside their desk job. I'd post more practical guides.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think I'd lose the claims job around 2030. But I could finish an electric vehicle course by then and work with Tomás. That would last until about 2034, maybe longer if I end up on the diagnostic side.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do an evening electric vehicle course next year and keep my claims job. I'd keep the bookkeeping too. I'd try to save a month of expenses before switching.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but hopeful. It feels like a plan, not a scramble.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you stay at the claims centre until then?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, as long as they'd keep me. I'd keep pushing to be the tool person. That buys time and pays the rent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would Tomás think?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He'd be proud, but he'd worry about us both working in the same place. If Tomás (my boyfriend) and I both work at the same garage and it goes under, we both go. That's the scary part.

People should learn **something hands-on** alongside their desk jobs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. That's more like a real career plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a big chance to rethink work. I'd tell people to take courses early and not wait for redundancy. I'd keep sharing tips online.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I'd be okay. I'd keep the claims job until around 2033 and move into electric vehicle diagnostics. That would last until 2039 or later.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do the fraud analytics course first, to boost my current job, then the electric vehicle course a few years later. I'd keep the bookkeeping and slowly build savings to two months.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy rather than anxious. It feels like I'd have time to do it properly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you still use AI daily?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Definitely. I'd use it to learn the car stuff too. I'd be the person who can read a fault code and explain it to the customer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell younger people?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Learn one skill that uses your hands and one that uses your head, so you've got two doors.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028. Even I'd struggle with that. What would help is paid training and some income support while we switch.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask about couples. When two people's jobs both change, it's different, because you have to plan together.

headlineQuote: When two people's jobs both change, it's different, because you have to plan together.
portrait: Aisha is a **27-year-old health claims processor** at a big claims centre.
She uses AI **daily** and tests new tools for her team.
She and Tomás, a **mechanic**, have about two weeks of savings.
Her plan moves from **fraud review** to electric vehicle repair as time shortens.
She's pragmatic and **adaptive**, but fast AGI alarms her.
